articles.title: Russia backs Trump's energy truce plan with Ukraine, seeks sanctions relief
articles.summary: Europe News: The Kremlin on Tuesday welcomed US President Donald Trump’s proposal for Russia and Ukraine to stop striking each other’s energy facilities, but said .
articles.body: The Kremlin on Tuesday welcomed US President Donald Trump’s proposal for Russia and Ukraine to stop striking each other’s energy facilities, but said an energy truce alone would not be enough to bring down fuel prices worldwide.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow considered Trump’s proposal a “very good idea”. However, he said other issues, including the safety of oil shipments and sanctions on Russia, also needed to be addressed.Trump had said on Monday that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to halt attacks on energy targets. Russia and Ukraine have not confirmed the agreement. On the same day, Russia struck petrol stations in Kyiv, while Ukraine said it had targeted a Russian oil refinery.Peskov said Russia would continue discussions with the US on Trump’s proposal.“It is necessary to ensure safe commercial shipping and navigation here, including for oil tankers. The Kyiv regime has so far shown no inclination to guarantee such security,” Peskov said.He also called for sanctions against Russia to be lifted, arguing that this would help stabilise energy supplies and global markets.“And the second thing that needs to be done is, of course, to lift sanctions (against Russia) and these unlawful restrictions on energy supplies. Only then will the world be adequately supplied with these petroleum products, global markets will stabilise, and prices will move lower.”Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was willing to back an energy ceasefire, but only if the US could establish that Russia was genuinely prepared to stop the war.The issue has gained importance as attacks on energy infrastructure have affected fuel supplies. Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities have contributed to shortages of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel in Russia, forcing Moscow to limit some exports.Ukraine, which has also faced repeated Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure, maintains that Russian refineries are legitimate military targets.Trump on Sunday called on Zelenskyy to stop attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the strikes were causing a diesel shortage that was “hurting the world”.The Kremlin, meanwhile, has blamed the wider disruption in global energy markets mainly on the conflict in the Gulf.Trump launched military strikes on Iran in February, following which Tehran largely shut the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway had been used to transport about one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies.The Russia-Ukraine conflict has also spread to commercial shipping. Both sides have targeted cargo vessels in the Black and Azov seas, adding to pressure on global grain prices as Russia and Ukraine are among the world’s major grain exporters.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Developers once planned Adirondack Park’s largest residential project on 5,800 New York acres; after years of failure and foreclosure litigation, the land is headed for public auction
articles.summary: US News: After years of legal wrangling, the 5,800-acre tract in New York’s Adirondack Park that was once planned for residential development is now headed for.
articles.body: After years of legal wrangling, the 5,800-acre tract in New York’s Adirondack Park that was once planned for residential development is now headed for a public foreclosure auction. The property, near Simond Pond and the former Big Tupper ski centre, will be auctioned on 18 September at the Franklin County Courthouse in Malone, according to a report by Times Union.The land was once pitched as the largest residential development in the Adirondack Park’s history. The Adirondack Club and Resort was a project that promised hundreds of second homes, a hotel, hiking trails, and the return of the long-closed Big Tupper ski area. More than a decade after receiving regulatory approval, the project remains unfinished as the property’s ownership has become tied up in a lengthy foreclosure dispute.The major residential project that never took offThe original vision sounded plausible enough. In 2012, the Adirondack Park Agency signed off on permits for the Adirondack Club and Resort. The plan was to construct 600 luxury ‘second homes’, a renovated marina, a reopened ski centre, and scattered hiking trails across the massive piece of land. The developer group, Preserve Associates, had successfully cleared a high regulatory bar after contentious public hearings.However, the environmental groups weren’t convinced. Protect the Adirondacks and the Sierra Club sued to block the project. They called it ‘the greatest threat to the ecological integrity of the Adirondack Park since the creation of the Adirondack Park Agency’. But they lost, and the permits stuck.In 2017, Preserve Associates bought the land from the Oval Wood Dish Liquidating Trust for $5.2 million. The property had once supplied lumber to the region’s woodenware factory. Now it was supposed to become a playground for the affluent.But things worsened quickly. Preserve Associates couldn’t sustain mortgage payments. The Oval Wood Dish Liquidating Trust, which held the original loan, watched the debt go into default. That’s when Stanley Hutton Rumbough, an investor and businessman with long-standing ties to the Tupper Lake area, stepped in. He bought the mortgage in 2019 and filed for foreclosure. But what followed was a cascade of litigation. Creditors of Preserve Associates launched disputes. And in all this, seven years went by. The parcel that was supposed to be the iconic residential development sat idle. But Rumbough continued to believe in it. He purchased the Blue Jay Campgrounds and Marina on the lake itself for $2.5 million and began upgrades. He started discussions with developers on how to either build the residential project or reopen the ski centre, or possibly both. That gamble is why the Tupper Lake project still has value despite its troubled history.It’s a calculated gamble that the Tupper Lake project, despite its tattered history, still holds value for someone willing to bet on it. A State Supreme Court-appointed referee has now determined that Rumbough is owed $10.58 million, plus interest, for money spent in connection with the property. The auction is intended to move the foreclosure process forward and provide a way for the outstanding obligations to be resolved. Rumbough could bid for the acreage himself. He has also been discussing the possibility of reviving the residential development with other developers, according to Jay Creutz, manager of Crossroads ADK LLC, the mortgage holder. Franklin County is also owed more than $1 million in property taxes and penalties.Whether a new owner can actually build depends partly on the APA permits that Preserve Associates secured over a decade ago. Creutz noted that the permits transfer with the land, and a new buyer could theoretically pick up where the original developers left off. However, Claudia Braymer, executive director of Protect the Adirondacks, is uncertain whether the rules still apply. There is a question as to whether a new buyer can simply start building now. The answer could define what happens next. The environmental concerns raised in 2012 haven’t disappeared yet.The former ski centre is also involved in the area’s changing ownership scenario, although it is no longer included in the upcoming sale of the 5,800 acres. In 2024, New Jersey investors Josh Parnes and Martin Schapira, operating as Love Tupper LLC, purchased smaller parcels from the original development site at a separate foreclosure auction. They paid $650,000 for Mount Morris, home to the former ski centre, and have purchased other local properties, including the Trails End tavern, which they remodelled and recently reopened.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'One inspection, all Noida schools shut?': Education department fact-checks Saurav Das's claim
articles.summary: NOIDA: A claim by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) spokesperson Saurav Das that all government schools in Uttar Pradesh’s Gautam Buddh Nagar district were .
articles.body: NOIDA: A claim by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) spokesperson Saurav Das that all government schools in Uttar Pradesh’s Gautam Buddh Nagar district were ordered to shut immediately after his team inspected a school in Noida has been refuted by the district education department.In a post on X, Das claimed that all government schools in Gautam Buddh Nagar had been directed to close immediately and linked the alleged action to the CJP’s inspection of a school in Noida.He also questioned what the Uttar Pradesh government was trying to hide.However, the District Basic Education Officer (DBEO), Gautam Buddh Nagar, said the claim was false and misleading and clarified that no such closure order had been issued.In an office order issued on Tuesday, DBEO Rahul Panwar said a misleading message had been circulated on social media by Das stating: "All government Schools in Gautam Buddh Nagar in UP have been directed to be CLOSED immediately."The officer said the statement was "completely false/misleading" and was being thoroughly refuted."All council schools (government primary/upper primary schools) in Gautam Buddh Nagar district are functioning as per the timetable set by the administration and the department, and no order regarding the closure of any school has been issued," Panwar said in the order.The clarification came after the CJP took its ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign to Noida on Tuesday.Das had announced an audit of schools in the city and urged young people across Uttar Pradesh to inspect schools in their neighbourhoods.Das had said the team would visit schools in Noida to assess the conditions in which children were studying and document its findings.He also said Noida was considered one of the better districts in Uttar Pradesh and that the team would assess whether its schools matched that perception.The CJP spokesperson had also appealed to young people in Uttar Pradesh to conduct school audits in their respective areas and document the condition of schools and the education being provided to children.The CJP launched its nationwide ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign in August, describing it as a social-audit drive focused on government schools and basic facilities.Its first audit was conducted at a government school in Santuk Pimpri village of Maharashtra’s Hingoli district, where CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke highlighted issues including lack of drinking water, benches, dirty washrooms, broken windows and inadequate water supply.Subsequent CJP audits have also focused on classrooms, drinking-water facilities, toilets, articles.title: 'BJP, RSS trying to impose Hindu law on non-Hindus': Owaisi on Amit Shah's UCC push
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday turned to the Constitution to counter Union home minister Amit Shah's push to implement the Unifo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday turned to the Constitution to counter Union home minister Amit Shah's push to implement the Uniform Civil Code in all 21 NDA-ruled states by 2029. Hyderabad MP said that the Bhartiya Janata Party is using the proposed law to target Muslims and arguing that it could undermine key constitutional protections.Speaking to the media in Bhopal, Owaisi said the proposed law would conflict with several provisions of the Constitution.“This is against Articles 25, 26, 14 and 29 of the Constitution, and you cannot implement such a law by abolishing freedom of religion,” AIMIM leader said.His remarks came a day after he attacked Union home minister Amit Shah and the BJP over their push for the UCC.Speaking to reporters in Hyderabad on Monday, Owaisi alleged that the BJP was not seeking the UCC in the interest of equality but to target India’s Muslim population."First, you need to understand that the BJP is not pursuing the UCC for the sake of equality. They have introduced the UCC in their states and at the government level solely to target India's 18 crore Muslims; in doing so, the BJP and Amit Shah are acting in contravention of Articles 25 (Freedom of Religion), 14 (Right to Equality), 26, and 29 of the Indian Constitution. So, one must first grasp that this move by the BJP is not about equality; it is purely to target Muslims," Owaisi told reporters.Owaisi also stressed that pluralism was central to India’s identity and cited an earlier Law Commission report on the UCC."Secondly, the very soul and spirit of this country is pluralism. Thirdly, Amit Shah, the BJP, and the RSS are attempting to impose Hindu law upon non-Hindus. Fourthly, the Law Commission-constituted by the Modi government itself-stated in its report that the UCC is neither necessary nor desirable for India," the AIMIM chief said.He further alleged that Shah, the BJP and the RSS were trying to impose Hindu law on non-Hindus.The UCC seeks to bring a common set of personal laws for all citizens, regardless of religion, covering matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption.The issue has remained a key BJP agenda, with the party pitching it as part of its wider legal and social reform programme.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Chinese village collected plastic from its mangroves and turned the waste into silk-like scarves for volunteers, linking cleanup with recycling
articles.summary: China News: In Tantou Village, in Nansha District of Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, mangroves were once little more than ordinary shoreline plants to many residen.
articles.body: In Tantou Village, in Nansha District of Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, mangroves were once little more than ordinary shoreline plants to many residents. Huang Jinhua, the village's Party secretary, recalled growing up catching fiddler crabs and river shrimp along the beach without giving much thought to the mangroves around them. That changed in 2019, when a powerful typhoon struck the area, and the water level rose so quickly that villagers began preparing to evacuate. But the tide eventually receded, prompting residents to recognise the role the mangroves played as natural coastal protection. The village began organising regular beach cleanups and carrying out pest and disease control for the plants. What started as a local effort later grew into a more organised conservation programme involving researchers, volunteers, students and residents. The village now recycles plastic collected from its mangroves into silk-like scarves, which are given to volunteers as a reminder of their efforts.How a tense encounter with researchers turned into a scientific partnershipThe village's conservation work became more systematic after an unexpected encounter in 2022. During a routine patrol, residents spotted a group of strangers near the mangrove forest and immediately became suspicious. They approached the visitors and warned them not to cut the trees. The strangers turned out to be researchers from the Guangzhou Marine Carbon Peaking and Carbon Neutrality Research Association, who had travelled to Tantou to survey the mangroves. The researchers had previously identified the forest using drones and remote sensing technology and found that although the mangroves were growing well, the area lacked proper scientific management. The misunderstanding quickly turned into cooperation. With support from the United Nations Development Programme, the association helped build a 300-metre mangrove science corridor in 2023, featuring 46 display panels along the wetland. The corridor gave the village a way to explain the ecosystem to visitors while connecting local conservation work with scientific research. Instead of viewing outside researchers with suspicion, residents began working with them to better understand and protect the mangroves. The partnership also brought more organised environmental education into the village.How the village turned its library into a marine science baseThe new partnership encouraged residents to become more involved themselves. Song Meiying, Tantou's deputy Party secretary, said seeing a public welfare organisation travel so far specifically to help protect the mangroves inspired the village to increase its own efforts. One part of that response was transforming the local library into a marine science base containing more than 1,000 specialised books. The village also formed a volunteer team of more than 50 local women and children who serve as science interpreters for visitors. Academics have joined the effort as well. Liang Xiaoting, an associate professor at Guangdong Eco-Engineering Polytechnic, became involved after being moved by the mangroves during a summer cleanup. She spontaneously picked up a microphone and began explaining the ecological value of mangroves to people nearby. Liang now regularly volunteers in Nansha and leads her students in developing ecological courses for primary and secondary schools.Why the village decided collecting trash was not enoughRegular beach cleanups eventually showed residents and researchers that simply removing rubbish from the wetland was not enough. That led to a "waste-to-wealth" initiative in which plastic collected from the mangroves was recycled into silk-like scarves. The scarves are given to volunteers as a tangible reminder of their contribution to the cleanups. The programme has also brought volunteers from beyond Tantou. Huang said people now travel from across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area to take part in beach cleanups, including many young people from Hong Kong and Macao. With more people visiting the wetland for cleanups and field research, local leaders are considering a small station near the mangroves where volunteers and researchers can rest.How Tantou's mangrove work fits into China's wider conservation effortTantou's experience comes as China's mangrove coverage has grown nationally. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period from 2021 to 2025, China's mangrove area expanded to 465,000 mu, or about 31,000 hectares, making China one of the few countries in the world to record a net increase in mangrove coverage during the period. Mangroves, alongside seagrass and coral reefs, are recognised globally as one of the three main marine coastal ecosystems. They support offshore fisheries, help purify the surrounding environment and contribute to carbon sequestration.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: At 22, Jayden Williams became Stockbridge’s youngest mayor; 10 months later, the city council removed him after a 10-hour misconduct hearing
articles.summary: US News: Jayden Williams made history as the youngest mayor of Stockbridge when he took office at age 22 in January. Just 10 months later, the city council vot.
articles.body: Jayden Williams made history as the youngest mayor of Stockbridge when he took office at age 22 in January. Just 10 months later, the city council voted to remove him from office following a 10-hour misconduct hearing focused on his administrative conduct, spending and use of city resources. According to local reports, Williams, now 23, was removed after the council reviewed evidence gathered during a months-long investigation. The council’s decision ended a difficult investigation into Williams’ use of public funds, city property and communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Mayor Pro Tem Elton Alexander has taken over as interim mayor while city officials prepare for a special election to fill the vacant position. Atlanta News First reported that the city is preparing a formal resolution declaring the mayor’s seat vacant.Allegations of Financial MismanagementThe hearing lasted from about 9:00 a.m. until nearly 9:00 p.m. City attorneys and investigators presented evidence about Williams’ handling of public money. A major part of the case involved allegations that Williams repeatedly used city purchasing cards for personal expenses. According to evidence presented during the hearing and reported by WSB-TV, the disputed charges included:Lyft rides, haircuts and movie ticketsPersonal clothing and tailoring servicesSeveral restaurant visits and meal chargesInvestigators also focused on a $322.92 charge made on Father’s Day at Pandora on the Square in McDonough. According to the city’s investigation documents, Williams originally listed the purchase as gift cards for city staff and later said the items had been given to community members. He also filed a form saying the original receipt was missing. Investigators later obtained the receipt. It showed that the $322.92 was spent on beverages and Father’s Day meals for Williams’ family, according to the evidence presented by the city.Williams defended himself during the hearing, saying he did not intentionally use the city card for personal purchases. He also argued that many of the disputed transactions were connected to official city business. WSB-TV reported that Williams said he reimbursed the city for some of the expenses. When questioned about Stockbridge’s purchasing and ethics policy, Williams testified that he had not read it. He said he had not received a copy when he took office, although he had asked for information about the rules after being elected. WSB-TV reported that Williams also maintained that he had not received proper training on the city’s policies.Misuse of City Assets and PersonnelThe investigation also examined Williams’ use of a city-owned vehicle and fuel cards. According to evidence presented during the hearing, Williams had a city vehicle checked out for 183 days between January and June. The city said this accounted for all but nine days of his early time in office. Local reporting also noted that the city’s rules require municipal vehicles to be used for official business or emergencies. Williams disputed the city’s interpretation of his vehicle use. Earlier, he said the vehicle remained available to him but that he was not necessarily using it every day. His attorney also argued that Williams had not received comprehensive training on the city’s vehicle policies. The city also presented evidence that Williams accumulated about $2,600 in fuel expenses using a city card during the same period, according to WSB-TV.The hearing also examined Williams’ communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Evidence presented to the council included text messages exchanged in late November and early December, before Williams took office, as well as additional messages sent in January. Reports said the communications included sexually suggestive messages and allegations involving explicit photographs. Police reviewed the communications but did not bring criminal charges. The student was 18 and therefore legally an adult under Georgia law. However, the city continued to examine the matter as a possible violation of the conduct standards expected of an elected official. Williams has said the communications took place before he became mayor. In a previous statement reported by FOX 5 Atlanta, he said the individual was 18 at the time and had never taken part in the city’s “Mayor for a Day” program. City Attorney Quinton Washington said the council considered the evidence as a whole before deciding to remove Williams. “When taken in concert together, the employee treatment, all of those things were things that they felt like did not uphold the standard that Stockbridge would like to see in its mayor,” Washington said.Defense Claims Personal GrudgeAfter the council’s vote, Mayor Pro Tem Elton Alexander defended the decision, saying officials had a responsibility to protect the city and its residents. “The results of the investigation demanded we act,” Alexander said. Alexander also confirmed that he does not plan to run in the special election to permanently replace Williams.“I have no desire to be mayor,” Alexander said. “For me to run for mayor means giving up my ability to vote, and I would never do that.” Williams and his attorney, Robert Kenner, strongly disagreed with the council’s decision. They argued that council members were biased against the mayor and had already made up their minds before the hearing.Kenner said the decision was not supported by sufficient evidence and accused the council of acting because of a personal dispute with Williams. “What happened tonight was very disappointing,” Kenner said. “I don’t believe that it was based on any evidence. I think it was based on a personal grudge against the mayor.”Kenner said Williams has the right to challenge the council’s decision in court. He indicated that the legal team would consider an appeal in Henry County Superior Court. The proceedings had already faced legal challenges before the final vote. Councilwoman LaKeisha Gantt was barred from participating after a judge found that her previous communications showed bias against Williams. The judge’s decision followed evidence involving messages and other communications between Gantt and people connected to the mayor.Gantt therefore did not take part in the final removal decision, according to CBS Atlanta. The city is now preparing for a special election to choose Williams’ replacement. Atlanta News First reported that officials are working on the formal steps needed to declare the mayor’s seat vacant and begin the election process. Officials are also expected to determine whether Williams will legally be allowed to run again.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Real' Sena case in SC: Shinde camp backs EC’s ‘organisational majority’ test
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday resumed final hearing on pleas challenging the Maharashtra Speaker’s refusal to disqualify MLAs of the Eknath .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday resumed final hearing on pleas challenging the Maharashtra Speaker’s refusal to disqualify MLAs of the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena faction, with the group defending the Election Commission’s decision to recognise it as the “real” Shiv Sena.A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana is also hearing the Uddhav Thackeray faction’s challenge to the EC’s February 17, 2023, order allotting the Shiv Sena name and ‘bow-and-arrow’ symbol to the Shinde camp.‘EC can examine party structure’Senior advocate Neeraj Kishan Kaul, appearing for the Shinde faction, argued that the EC was empowered under Article 324 to examine a party’s constitution and organisational structure while deciding which faction represented the real party.“Your Lordships must see the entire record. The question is whether the constitution was with the Election Commission,” Kaul said.He said the constitution relied upon by the Thackeray faction was not registered with the EC, while the 1999 constitution was submitted after detailed correspondence with the poll panel.Kaul said the EC was not deciding which amendments could be made to the constitution but whether the organisational structure reflected the will of the party cadre.‘It was a political party split’Rejecting the argument that the dispute was limited to a split in the legislative wing, Kaul said, “Our case has never been that there was merely a split in the legislative party. Our case is that there was a split in the political party.”He defended the EC’s organisational majority test, saying it could not conduct a referendum among every primary member of a political party.“The lifeblood of a political party is its cadre and grassroots workers who are directly connected to the electorate,” Kaul said.The hearing remained inconclusive and will continue on Wednesday.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: How fish has BJP's plate full in West Bengal
articles.summary: India News: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari last week offered prayers at the Kalighat Temple on the occasion of 'Kaushiki Amavasya' and partook of a t.
articles.body: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari last week offered prayers at the Kalighat Temple on the occasion of 'Kaushiki Amavasya' and partook of a traditional bhog that included fish and 'basanti pulao'. Interestingly, the timing of the visit gave the ritual a political context.The meal came amid a political controversy over Bageshwar Dham chief Dhirendra Krishna Shastri's recent appeal to Bengali Hindus to refrain from eating non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja. As expected, the remarks kicked up a political storm, forcing the BJP’s Bengal unit to publicly distinguish itself from Dhirendra Shastri’s position on food.Chief minister Adhikari, who had shared a stage with Shastri earlier this month and invited him to establish a centre in Bengal, then got into the balancing act.“A religious figure is entitled to express his opinion, but whether people accept it or not is a personal matter,” the chief minister said after his Kalighat visit.Adhikari also referred to his own practices, saying he follows a sattvik diet on Ashtami and during Kartik, while accepting fish offered to Goddess Kali as bhog and goat meat as prasad."A saint or a religious leader is entitled to express their opinion. People may choose to accept it or not. On Mahashtami, when I worship Maa Durga, I consume sattvik food. During the month of Kartik also, I consume sattvik food. At the same time, as a Bengali, I accept the bhog offered to Maa with fish. I also accept the prasad of goat sacrifice. Today, whatever was offered to Maa in the afternoon, the temple priests gave me the same. There was fish head and fried fish, along with basanti pulao," he said.From Liluah to KalighatAll this began on September 4, when Adhikari shared the stage with Shastri at a Hanumant Katha programme at the Liluah Workshop Ground in Howrah.Addressing Shastri, Adhikari said: "Baba Maharaj Ji, please open a centre here. There should also be a Bageshwar Dham centre. This is the land of saints and of spiritual awakening."Two days later, on September 6, Shastri appealed to Hindus in Bengal not to sell, cook or eat non-vegetarian food near Durga Puja idols during Navratri. He described those consuming such food as "pakhandi" and called for opposition to the practice."I am appealing to the Hindus of Bengal, that during Navratri, even if you don't keep the idols of the Goddess, do not sell or consume non-veg near the idols. I do not like it when dirty non-vegetarian food is eaten during Durga Puja and at gatherings linked to the festivities. I want the Hindus of Kolkata to awaken and boycott such people. These people cannot be considered religious; they are pakhandi (hypocrites). Wake up and expel those people," he appealed.BJP pushbackThe remarks triggered criticism from the opposition and prompted the Bengal BJP to distance itself from the dietary prescription.State BJP president Samik Bhattacharya said no one could decide what Bengalis should eat."How can Bengalis not have fish and meat?" he said, adding that people in Bengal would continue with their traditional food practices. He also invoked Swami Vivekananda while defending the consumption of meat and fish in Bengal’s religious traditions.Other BJP leaders, including Dilip Ghosh, also said food choices were a matter of personal preference and referred to the place of meat in some Bengali religious traditions.The Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) also found itself navigating the controversy following statements made during an interactive session with Kolkata puja organizers. Swami Nirgunananda, a member of the VHP's central advisory council, had suggested that non-vegetarian food stalls be kept away from the immediate area around Durga idols and situated in designated spaces outside pandals to maintain sanctity and cleanliness.When his comments were interpreted as an official organisational diktat restricting meat sales, VHP International president Alok Kumar issued a formal clarification. "Vishva Hindu Parishad has not issued any directions regarding the arrangements at Durga Puja pandals... worship of the Goddess should take place according to tradition and the atmosphere should be one of love and devotion," it said.The Kalighat temple is associated with Bengal's 'Shakta' tradition, in which offerings can include fish and meat. The bhog included several varieties of fish, along with other vegetarian dishes and goat meat.That tradition sits somewhat differently from the vegetarian dietary practices associated with Navratri in several parts of north and west India.The not-so-new ‘maach-bhaat’ rowThe controversy over Shastri's remarks comes months after fish and meat had already become part of the BJP-TMC contest over Bengali identity during the assembly election campaign.Mamata Banerjee repeatedly alleged during the campaign that a BJP government would restrict what Bengalis could eat. At a rally in Purulia on March 29, she said: "BJP says can't eat fish, meat, eggs." She subsequently argued that restrictions on meat and fish sales in some BJP-ruled states showed what could lie ahead for Bengal.The issue became prominent enough for senior BJP leaders to address it directly. Amit Shah clarified that "consumption of fish, eggs will not be stopped" if the BJP came to power in Bengal, calling Mamata's claim a rumour.Prime Minister Narendra Modi also sought to engage with the issue, though from a different direction. At a rally in Haldia, he spoke about Bengal's fish production and said the state could become self-sufficient in fish under a BJP government. "In 15 years, TMC couldn't even give you fish. We created a separate ministry for fisheries," he said, contrasting Bengal's production with that of Bihar and Assam.The BJP’s campaign also included more visible efforts to counter the perception that it was opposed to Bengali food habits. Leaders publicly ate fish and meat, while BJP candidates and workers used fish in campaign imagery. On Poila Boishakh, TMC organised a "Maach-Bhaat-e-Bangali" procession, alleging that the BJP would impose restrictions on fish and meat.The argument did not remain confined to the two parties. TMC leaders presented food as part of the broader question of Bengali identity. BJP leaders, in turn, sought to emphasise that dietary choices would remain a matter of personal freedom.The Bengal and Bengali dilemma for SuvenduMonths after the BJP swept Bengal in assembly elections, the opposition has sought to use the same "outsider" charge to try and alienate the saffron party from the voters. Congress filed a police complaint against Shastri, alleging that his comments hurt Bengali sentiments, while invoking the “outsider” argument that the TMC had used against the BJP during the election. Congress’s complaint described his remarks as an affront to Bengali traditions and social harmony.The TMC, which had made fish and meat part of its cultural-identity campaign against the BJP, is also again using the remark against the party.As CM, however, Adhikari has also taken a position on protests against Shastri.On September 10, he directed the Kolkata Police commissioner to arrest those who allegedly burnt Shastri’s photographs during a protest in Bhawanipur. "Not in Bengal," he said, making clear that burning photographs as a form of protest would not be tolerated.The move has produced another political contest. Congress has criticised the arrests and accused the government of protecting Shastri while acting against those protesting his remarks. One Congress leader, Atanu Das, was subsequently arrested.The larger question for BJPThe recent row has brought an old question back for the BJP in Bengal: how does the party's Hindu politics sit with the state's own traditions?Bengal has a strong Shakta tradition, centred on Kali and Durga. In this tradition, the line between what is considered religious and what is considered non-vegetarian is not always drawn in the same way as it is in northern/western India. Fish, and in some places meat, can be part of offerings and rituals.That makes food an unusually sensitive issue in Bengal. And for many Bengalis, it is tied to family customs, festivals and a sense of what is distinctly 'Bengali'.Suvendu Adhikari is leading the first BJP government in Bengal. For now, he might be able to shut down critics by consuming fish bhog at Kalighat. But it will be interesting to see how he manages BJP's national Hindu politics in Bengal while also balancing the "Bengaliness".Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Penn’s Cave opened to visitors in 1885 and has been run by the same Pennsylvania family since 1908; after four generations, its owners want the 1,500-acre property to become a state park rather than be developed
articles.summary: US News: Long before tourists arrived by boat, Penn’s Cave was simply a dark opening in the Pennsylvania countryside. In 1795, an Irish pastor descended into t.
articles.body: Long before tourists arrived by boat, Penn’s Cave was simply a dark opening in the Pennsylvania countryside. In 1795, an Irish pastor descended into the hole and found a vast underground world of stalactites, stalagmites and icy water. More than two centuries later, the cave remains much as nature made it. Visitors now enter through a gift shop before boarding boats for a journey along the cold subterranean waters of Penns Creek, states an online report by The Philadelphia Inquirer. Above ground, the surrounding wildlife park stretches across hundreds of acres and is home to bison, wolves, elk and a particularly imposing black bear, adds the report. Today, the attraction draws thousands of visitors each year from its location just east of State College in Centre County. Now, however, its future may take an unexpected turn. Wondering why? Scroll down to find out.From family business to state parkPenn’s Cave and Wildlife Park opened to tourists in 1885 and has been operated by the same Pennsylvania family since 1908. After four generations, the owners are seeking to transfer the roughly 1,500-acre property to the state, potentially making it Pennsylvania’s 126th state park, states the online report. The proposal has emerged from years of discussions with the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, or DCNR. Centre County commissioners and State Rep. Kerry Benninghoff have backed the idea, with preservation at the heart of the proposal. For the Schleiden family, which currently owns and operates the attraction, the question is what happens to the property when the family is no longer in a position to run it? Keeping the land and cave protected would prevent the site from eventually being carved up for development.DCNR has already inspected the property and held discussions about potentially assuming stewardship of the cave and its surrounding natural and cultural resources. Any acquisition could require approval from the state legislature.A different kind of state parkPenn’s Cave would not fit neatly into the traditional state-park model. Pennsylvania’s newest state park, Laurel Caverns in Fayette County, also began as a privately operated cave attraction before being donated to the state. But the similarities largely end there. Visitors explore Laurel Caverns on foot, while Penn’s Cave is experienced from boats navigating an underground waterway filled with rainbow trout. The property above Penn’s Cave also presents a bigger management question. Its rolling farmland and wildlife enclosures cover a much larger area than Laurel Caverns. Whether the state would continue operating the existing animal exhibits, which include elk, Texas longhorns and mountain lions, remains uncertain. Camping could eventually become another possibility if the property enters the state park system, although that too would have to be determined, adds the report.Preserving more than a tourist attractionA state takeover would also raise practical questions about staffing, maintenance and operating costs. Penn’s Cave currently employs both seasonal and full-time workers and operates visitor facilities including a gift shop and snack stand. Yet the central issue is bigger than the future of a tourism business.Inside the cave, the formations have taken thousands of years to develop. Its underground waterways and geology are part of Pennsylvania’s natural heritage, while the surrounding landscape provides habitat and recreational space. For a family that has cared for the property for four generations, turning Penn’s Cave into a state park could be a way of ensuring that its next chapter is defined not by development, but by preservation.For now, the boats still leave from the dock, visitors still descend into the darkness, and Penn’s Cave remains a family-run attraction waiting to learn whether its future will ultimately belong to the state.Image Courtesy: The Philadelphia InquirerCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump slams 3 justices he nominated after mail-voting setback: ‘Not the people I interviewed’

articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday attacked the Supreme Court after it rejected his administration’s push to restrict mail-in voting in this year’s midterm elections, saying the justices who ruled against him were “not the people I interviewed.”The court, in an emergency order late Monday, found that the restrictions would likely not withstand legal scrutiny, at least for this year’s election.‘Not enough time’ for mail ballot changesThe Trump administration had made a last-minute push for the US Postal Service to play a central role in determining who could receive mail ballots. But state election officials argued there was not enough time to implement the changes before the November 3 midterm elections, saying existing systems were already secure and accurate.Trump, however, accused the court of failing to “do the right thing” for the country and said its decision would be remembered negatively in history.‘These are not the people I interviewed’In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the Supreme Court was being “bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left” into making decisions that had “set America back at least a hundred years.”Three justices nominated by Trump during his first term — Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh — also ruled against his administration in Monday’s decision.“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” Trump said.He further accused the court of issuing “shockingly bad rulings” that he claimed were costing the US “Trillions of Dollars” and could make it difficult for the country to “recover or heal.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump promises $5,000 for every American adult: How will it affect US economy
articles.summary: US News: US president Donald Trump on Wednesday promised a $5,000 payment to every American adult if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate in.
articles.body: US president Donald Trump on Wednesday promised a $5,000 payment to every American adult if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate in the November midterm elections, in a striking bid to bolster his party’s weakening electoral position.“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”“We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money, we don’t want you going to China, to Germany. You gotta spend the money in the United States of America," Trump added.Within an hour of Trump’s announcement, Vice President JD Vance appeared to partially walk back the proposal, suggesting that the $5,000 dividend would not be paid to wealthy Americans.Vance also suggested that the payments could be funded through US tariff revenues, although the proposed dividend far exceeds the amount the US has collected so far through the tariffs, as cited by news agency AP.How would the "Trump Dividend" be funded?Trump did not provide details on how the proposed payments would be financed. Unless the government raises taxes, cuts spending elsewhere or generates sufficient additional revenue to cover the cost, the initiative would likely have to be funded through additional borrowing, as reported by Bloomberg.Last year, Trump had proposed $2,000 “dividend” payments for low- and middle-income Americans, to be financed through revenue from his sweeping tariffs on US goods imports. However, the proposal did not materialise.How will it affect the US economy?The proposal could add to concerns over the US national debt, which surpassed $40 trillion for the first time in recent weeks and has been putting upward pressure on borrowing costs.Economists and policymakers have also raised concerns that placing $5,000 in the hands of every US adult could fuel consumer spending and add to inflationary pressures. Prices have already risen amid Trump’s policies on Iran and tariffs, with gasoline and diesel costs particularly straining household budgets, as cited by Bloomberg.The proposed “Trump Dividend” comes as Trump faces a challenging political landscape ahead of the midterm elections. Polls show his popularity at record lows, while Americans across the political spectrum have expressed concerns over his handling of the war in Iran and the economy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Our father being slowly killed': Imran Khan's sons accuse Pakistan's Asim Munir of vendetta
articles.summary: Pakistan News: The sons of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan have accused army chief Asim Munir of pursuing a \"personal vendetta\" against their father.
articles.body: The sons of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan have accused army chief Asim Munir of pursuing a "personal vendetta" against their father, alleging that his prison conditions amount to mental and physical torture.Speaking to The Guardian, Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, said they were “deeply” concerned about the health of their 73-year-old father, who has been held at Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023.Khan is serving a 14-year sentence in a corruption case. His sons said they had not been allowed to speak to him for more than six months and had also been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to seek his release.The allegations come ahead of a Supreme Court ruling on Wednesday in a case alleging that the Pakistan government has failed to comply with a court order allowing Khan private hospital treatment for an eye condition and permitting family visits and communication.Sulaiman alleged that his father had been denied human contact, new books, access to family and an independent doctor. He also said Khan’s eye condition had been neglected for months, potentially resulting in severe loss of sight in one eye."It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge," Sulaiman told The Guardian, alleging that Khan was being treated harshly on Munir’s orders.Khan had reportedly demoted Munir during his tenure as prime minister, and tensions between the two were widely known. Munir became army chief in 2022, while Khan’s political conflict with the military establishment intensified.Kasim alleged that the family believed their father was being “slowly killed” in prison and said they feared restrictions on him could become harsher when international pressure eased.The allegations follow a recent dispute over Khan’s medical treatment. Last month, the Supreme Court ruled that he should be taken to a private hospital for treatment of a blood clot in a retinal vein. His family said the condition had severely affected the sight in his right eye.Khan was instead briefly taken to a government hospital, where he received injections before being declared fit to return to prison, according to The Guardian.The Pakistan government has rejected the allegations, calling them “fake propaganda”. It said Khan was being kept in adequate conditions and had access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” it said.The United Nations has previously said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law, while the UN special rapporteur on torture has said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lalbaugcha Raja: How a broken market, struggling fishermen and a vow to Lord Ganesha created Mumbai’s most famous Ganpati
articles.summary: Mumbai’s most famous Ganpati did not begin with a grand pandal or celebrity crowds. Its story began with a market that had shut down, families worried.
articles.body: Mumbai’s most famous Ganpati did not begin with a grand pandal or celebrity crowds. Its story began with a market that had shut down, families worried about their livelihood and a promise made to Lord Ganesha. In 1934, that promise took the form of an idol. More than nine decades later, Lalbaugcha Raja remains one of Mumbai’s most powerful symbols of faith and community.When a market disappeared, so did livelihoodsIn 1932, a market near Peru Chawl in Lalbaug was shut down. The closure affected vendors, traders and fishermen, including members of the local Koli community who depended on the area for their livelihood.The community wanted a permanent marketplace. They prayed for a place where they could continue their trade. Their wish was eventually fulfilled when land was made available for a permanent market, which became the present Lalbaug Market.A vow became Lalbaugcha RajaThe community’s gratitude became a religious promise, or navas. In September 1934, the traders and fishermen installed a public Ganesha idol dressed in the traditional attire of a fisherman.The Lalbaugcha Raja Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal was established in 1934. The idol soon became associated with the idea of a Navsacha Ganpati, or Ganesha believed to fulfil devotees’ wishes.That origin gives the festival a meaning that goes beyond spectacle. At its heart is a very ordinary human hope: finding work, stability and a place to belong.The Kambli family gave the Raja his familiar faceThe idol’s distinctive form has another remarkable story. The Kambli family has been making the Lalbaugcha Raja idol since 1935, when Madhusudan Donduji Kambli began the tradition. Three generations of the family have since carried the work forward.In 2011, Kambli Arts secured intellectual-property protection for the traditional design, after replicas of the famous idol became increasingly common.So the Raja seen today is not simply a yearly sculpture. It carries a recognisable artistic tradition that has been carefully passed down.Why millions still stand in lineThe scale of Lalbaugcha Raja today is almost difficult to imagine. The idol is widely reported to attract around 1.5 million devotees a day during the festival.There are separate arrangements for Mukh Darshan and Charan Sparsh or Navsachi darshan. Long queues, sometimes stretching for many hours, have become part of the Lalbaug experience.The Maharashtra Tourism Department describes Ganesh Chaturthi as a festival that brings together devotion, culture and community life. Lalbaugcha Raja is perhaps one of Mumbai’s clearest examples of that idea.92 years completed, 93rd year beginsThe mandal is celebrating its 93rd year in 2026, with the festival running from September 14 to September 25.There is, however, one detail often missed in retellings of the story. The annual celebration was not literally held without interruption. In 2020, the mandal cancelled its traditional festivities during the COVID-19 pandemic and instead focused on awareness activities.That interruption does not weaken the story. If anything, it makes the history more human. Lalbaugcha Raja began with people asking for a livelihood, survived generations of change and continues to bring strangers together every Ganesh Chaturthi.Disclaimer: Historical accounts of Lalbaugcha Raja contain traditional narratives alongside documented records. Details such as the navas and its wish-fulfilling reputation reflect community belief and should not be treated as independently verifiable supernatural claims.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Nigeria arrests Mexican national after anti-drug agency raids industrial-scale meth laboratory
articles.summary: Authorities in Nigeria have shut down an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory and arrested a Mexican citizen at Lagos airport, the country's anti-drug...
articles.body:
ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — Authorities in Nigeria have shut down an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory and arrested a Mexican citizen at Lagos airport, the country's anti-drug agency said on Tuesday.

Agency spokesman Femi Babafemi said Arturo Carrera Loaiza was arrested in connection with the laboratory, located at a construction site in southeast Ebonyi State, while trying to flee the West African country.

"The breakthrough follows months of painstaking investigation into a wider criminal network behind a string of clandestine drug laboratories uncovered in parts of the country this year," Babafemi said.

It is the second time this year that the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency has shut down a large-scale drugs operation. In May, authorities arrested members of an organized drug syndicate involving Nigerians and Mexicans in the southwestern region of the country.

Among the items recovered in the latest raid were methamphetamine, three empty dehydrators, and hundreds of kilograms of chemical compounds, including acetone, ethanol, chloride salt, and hydrochloric acid.

West and Central Africa have emerged as a hot spot for global trafficking and manufacturing of illicit drugs due to porous borders and corruption in recent years, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

articles.title: Brazil SC weighs probe into judge who jailed ex-president Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Brazil’s Supreme Court on Tuesday began deliberations on whether Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the trial against former President Jair Bolsonar.
articles.body: Brazil’s Supreme Court on Tuesday began deliberations on whether Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the trial against former President Jair Bolsonaro, should face an investigation in a graft case, adding to tensions ahead of the country’s October presidential election.Moraes is facing allegations raised by Justice André Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee. Outside the court, dozens of Bolsonaro supporters protested, demanding that Moraes step down or face impeachment by the Senate.Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin opened the session after a 40-minute delay by reading a federal police report unsealed by Mendonca last week. Fachin said he had scheduled the hearing to address “a difficult moment” for the court.“Disagreements are legitimate. Personal confrontations are not,” Fachin said.Graft probe linked to Banco MasterThe case centres on whether Moraes should be included in an investigation into the shuttered Banco Master, which has ensnared senior politicians and members of the judiciary.Mendonca last week unsealed documents showing that the bank’s jailed head, Daniel Vorcaro, sought legal advice from Moraes shortly before his arrest. The documents also showed that the bank had a 130 million reais ($23 million) contract with the law firm of Moraes’ wife.Moraes has denied any wrongdoing and accused Mendonca of pursuing a personal vendetta against him.The dispute comes as Brazil heads towards a closely watched presidential election in October, with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva expected to face Bolsonaro’s son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1998, Pittsburgh's last operating steel mill closed, leaving 178 riverfront acres vacant; 28 years later, 700,000 sq ft has been built or is underway for robotics, biotech, housing and parks
articles.summary: US News: For decades, 178 acres along the Monongahela River in Pittsburgh remained largely vacant after the collapse of the steel industry. The site was once h.
articles.body: For decades, 178 acres along the Monongahela River in Pittsburgh remained largely vacant after the collapse of the steel industry. The site was once home to the Jones & Laughlin Steel Pittsburgh Works, one of the city's major steel-making sites.The steel works closed in the 1980s as the steel industry declined, leaving the Hazelwood Green property unused for decades, according to Axios. Most of the old industrial structures were demolished in the 2000s, while preparations for a new development began in the 2010s.The redevelopment has taken time to gather pace. One of the first major projects was Mill 19, which was renovated and opened in 2019 as a tech-flex office space. However, development slowed for several years after that.Now, Hazelwood Green is seeing a new wave of construction, with robotics, life sciences, housing, sports and public spaces becoming part of the former industrial site. Developers say around 700,000 square feet has been developed or is currently being built since 2022.Robotics and biotech projectsCarnegie Mellon University's Robotics Innovation Center opened at Hazelwood Green this year. The facility is now one of the main features of the developing neighbourhood and is located next to a public plaza and park.Pitt's BioForge facility is also set to open this autumn. It will join the growing group of technology and life science projects at the site, including Mill 19.Several technology companies already have offices in Hazelwood Green. These include life science company ElevateBio, artificial intelligence company Hellbender and autonomous vehicle company Motional.The development is also moving beyond offices and research facilities. Woodlawn Lofts, the first apartment complex at Hazelwood Green, is under construction, with its first phase expected to open in December.The complex will have 160 residential units. These will include market-rate homes, affordable homes for low-income residents and units reserved for single parents who are working towards their degrees.700,000 square feet developedThe scale of the recent construction is considerably larger than the development seen during the first phase of the project.According to Tishman Speyer managing director Austin Gelbard, around 250,000 square feet was developed at Hazelwood Green between 2010 and 2022. Since 2022, around 700,000 square feet has been developed or is in the process of being built.The change is also visible in the site's public spaces. The Hazelwood Green park hosted movie nights this summer, bringing visitors to an area that was previously known mainly for its industrial past.The U.S. Steel Community Field has also started being used. It hosted its first high school football game recently, giving thousands of people a look at the developing neighbourhood.Gelbard said the public plaza and park next to the Robotics Innovation Center are expected to help shape Lytle Street as Hazelwood Green's main street as more retail and housing are added."We want to bring folks down to the site for something fun. There hasn't always been a reason to visit Hazelwood Green."More housing, technology and retail plannedDespite the recent construction, a large part of Hazelwood Green is still waiting to be developed.There are 58 acres of mixed-use space available at the southern end of the site. Gelbard said this area could eventually include more technology companies, light-industrial businesses and retail.The northern end has space for around 1,200 multifamily housing units, adding significantly to the residential development already under construction.The project has received support from several philanthropic groups. Gelbard said hundreds of millions of dollars have been donated by organisations including the Richard King Mellon Foundation, U.S. Steel and the Heinz Endowments to help drive development in the neighbourhood.Another small park is expected to open next month near the entrance to the U.S. Steel Community Field. According to Gelbard, it will act as an entrance to Hazelwood Green and help connect the development with Second Avenue in Hazelwood.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: France planted Douglas-fir forests; scientists later found streams draining the plantations had up to 10 times more nitrate
articles.summary: Europe News: Forests are often associated with clean water, but a study of Douglas-fir plantations in France and Luxembourg has found that the trees can be linked .
articles.body: Forests are often associated with clean water, but a study of Douglas-fir plantations in France and Luxembourg has found that the trees can be linked to much higher nitrate levels in nearby streams and groundwater. Researchers examined paired headwater catchments with different land covers, including Douglas-fir, spruce, deciduous forests, grassland, and clearcuts. The catchments were monitored for three to five years to understand how Douglas-fir affected water chemistry. The study published in ‘Environmental Pollution’ found that streams draining Douglas-fir catchments had nitrate concentrations two to ten times higher than streams draining other forest and grassland areas. Groundwater beneath Douglas-fir also recorded nitrate concentrations reaching 50 milligrams per litre.How did Douglas-fir plantations affect nitrate levels in nearby streamsThe study found that streams draining Douglas-fir catchments had noticeably higher nitrate levels than those flowing through areas with other land covers. Across the three study areas, nitrate concentrations in streams below Douglas-fir were two to ten times higher than those measured in streams associated with spruce, deciduous vegetation and grassland. At some sites, nitrate concentrations in Douglas-fir streams also reached levels similar to those found below clearcut areas.At Breuil in France, nitrate levels in the Douglas-fir subcatchment ranged from 3 to 21 milligrams per litre between 2019 and 2021. The researchers found that these elevated concentrations were connected to nitrate production and accumulation in soils beneath Douglas-fir plantations.What did the soil reveal about higher nitrate levels in streamsThe researchers also examined nitrate in soils to understand where the higher stream concentrations were coming from. Soil nitrate concentrations under Douglas-fir were higher than under the other land covers studied. Their levels were also similar to those measured in clearcut areas at the French sites. This indicated that Douglas-fir plantations were linked to excess nitrate production in the soil.This was important because soil nitrate concentration was linked to nitrate concentration in nearby streams. The findings supported the researchers' hypothesis that a substantial share of the excess nitrate produced in Douglas-fir soils was transferred through the soil profile and eventually reached surface waters.Why was groundwater beneath Douglas-fir plantations high in nitrateGroundwater measurements provided another indication of the effect associated with Douglas-fir plantations. Nitrate concentrations beneath Douglas-fir reached as high as 50 milligrams per litre. These concentrations were higher than those recorded under the other land covers examined in the study. The researchers connected the groundwater results with the nitrate accumulation observed in Douglas-fir soils. When nitrate production exceeds the ability of plants, microorganisms and other processes to retain or remove it, the excess can move through the soil with water.How does the soil nitrogen cycle contribute to higher nitrate levelsThe researchers focused on how Douglas-fir plantations affect the movement of nitrogen through forest soils. Nitrogen enters forest systems and is then transformed through processes including mineralisation, nitrification, plant uptake, microbial immobilisation and denitrification. The balance between these processes determines how much nitrate remains available to move through the soil.The study's results show that this balance was different beneath Douglas-fir plantations. Excess nitrate production appeared to exceed processes that would normally retain or remove it. Seasonal changes in nitrate concentrations also showed an imbalance between nitrate production and consumption.Different tree species may help balance nitrate levels in surface waterAlthough Douglas-fir catchments showed higher nitrate concentrations, the study found that the effect became weaker further downstream. The researchers attributed this reduction partly to dilution as water from different areas mixed. This finding notes that the impact of Douglas-fir on surface-water nitrate is not necessarily the same throughout an entire catchment.The researchers proposed that mixing tree species at the catchment scale could help reduce the effect of Douglas-fir plantations on nitrate concentrations in surface waters. Their findings also show that forested catchments cannot always be assumed to have low nitrate levels.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ms. Rachel calls out Ed Sheeran after Macklemore dropped from tour following Palestine support
articles.summary: Children’s YouTuber Ms. Rachel criticized reports that Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his ongoing tour because of the rapper’s pro-Palestinian advocacy. “Ed Sheeran is making a political statement to his fans when he does a concert to support Ukraine, but considers Palestine too dangerous and political,” Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote…
articles.body:
Children’s YouTuber Ms. Rachel criticized reports that Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his ongoing tour because of the rapper’s pro-Palestinian advocacy.

“Ed Sheeran is making a political statement to his fans when he does a concert to support Ukraine, but considers Palestine too dangerous and political,” Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote in a Tuesday Instagram post .

On Monday, Macklemore said that stadium owners — among them Robert Kraft of the New England Patriots — urged the British singer to oust him from the Loop Tour due to past comments about Palestine. The rapper has posted several images of himself donning the Palestinian flag and shared several infographics about Israel’s war in Gaza to social media.

Accurso herself has a history of activism. In April 2025, she put out a statement online responding to criticism she faced over her calls for the protection of Palestinian children. The YouTuber star has also spoken out against Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities, having read books to detainees in New Jersey’s Delaney Hall in June.

“All children have the right to food, water, medical care and education. All children should be protected from violence,” she wrote in her 2025 statement.

Per The Hollywood Reporter , pro-Israel groups went after Macklemore earlier this month after he called for a “free Palestine” during Sheeran’s Sept. 4 MetLife Stadium concert. Pop artist Pink criticized the rapper for his pro-Palestinian comments, allegedly pushing for his removal from the tour.

In his own Instagram post Tuesday, Sheeran said that tour promoters, not himself, chose to cut Macklemore from Loop.

“Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me,” the British singer wrote.

“Imagine being a Palestinian kid and seeing he did a concert for Ukraine but when over 20,000 Palestinian children are killed he’s silent,” Accurso wrote, referencing Sheeran’s March 2022 performance raising funds for Ukraine after Russia’s invasion.

When his opening act says Palestinians should be free and not in a genocide he lets a billionaire kick him off,” the children’s YouTuber continued.

In an Aug. 2022 Instagram post, Ukrainian band Antytila posed alongside Sheeran with the country’s flag, commending the pop star for “standing by Ukraine.”

“Thank you Ed and all the team! You are great people with huge hearts!” the band wrote.

In a post on Instagram, Macklemore said Sheeran “and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour,” alleging the singer had spoken to him about pro-Palestinian messaging “being hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with.”

The rapper wrote, “I told (Sheeran) if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and when I stood.”

The YouTuber echoed Macklemore in her Tuesday post, saying, “Palestinian kids have been so dehumanized that as they continue to be killed people debate about being political. It’s sick.”

This story was updated at 4:12 p.m. on Sept. 15, 2026.
